articles.title: Healey provides some breathing space but things still set to get worse for most
articles.text:
John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.

It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.

While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.

The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.

Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.

But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.

Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%

However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.

The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.

As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.

And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.

So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.

The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.

So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.

Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.

There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.

And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.

The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.

Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.

Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.

And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.

Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.

So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.

With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.

The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.

So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.

For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.

A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

articles.title: Ofcom outlines age verification for under-16s ahead of social media ban
articles.text:
Ofcom has set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.

Under the UK's social media ban - which is due to come into force in March next year - those under that age will be prevented from accessing ten of the biggest platforms, including Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

Many UK adults are also likely to have to confirm that they are not under-age by using one of the proposed measures, which are subject to government approval.

A similar ban was introduced in Australia last year but many children there have found ways to get round it. The UK says it intends to take a tougher approach.

Age verification below 18 is challenging because 16 and 17 year olds don't have credit cards or full driving licences, and may not have passports either. They can also look significantly older or younger than they are.

To address that challenge, Ofcom has - in addition to traditional forms of ID - recommended four methods that it says would be "highly effective" at gauging people's ages:

photo ID matching, where relevant information on a photo ID document such as a passport is checked against a live image taken during an age check

banking-based checks, which involves using the information a financial institution has on record regarding a user's age

face age estimation technology (which the regulator argues has recently improved)

digital ID services, which enable people to digitally prove who they are or provide information about themselves, such as their age

The BBC has asked three of the UK's biggest banks whether they would have a process for assisting with social media requests for age verification if it did become an official measure.

However, ultimately it will be up to the tech companies to figure out how to implement the checks: the onus is on social network providers to come up with their own solutions and comply.

Ofcom CEO Dame Melanie Dawes said the regulator was drawing on its experience in introducing tougher age checks for porn sites last year:

"What we've learned in introducing age checks across the porn industry is that actually what a lot of countries did before us was say you need to do it this way and they were very prescriptive and it didn't work," she told the BBC.

"So what we've said all along is here are things that can work, they must preserve privacy, they must protect people's data, but it's on you to put in place what you think works for you."

Some of the tech companies, including Meta, have called for age verification to be applied at device level, so that someone under-age would be automatically blocked from installing social media apps via app stores.

Meta told the BBC it already applies some methods recommended by Ofcom to enforce its user age requirements or place users in Teen Accounts settings.

But it said applying age checks at device-level, via app stores, could reduce the burden on people to have to repeatedly verify their age across multiple platforms.

This would place responsibility with Apple and Google, who between them operate most of the world's smartphones. Apple has already introduced age verification in the UK.

However Ofcom says that would not absolve the social network providers from doing their own checks as well.

The regulator said it didn't have a firm number for how many adults would need to prove they were not under age, but conceded that it would be a "large number of accounts" that social media companies would need to "deal with."

It has also acknowledged that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated", and some children would succeed in bypassing the age checks.

Dawes said making the ban work would be a joint effort.

"At Ofcom, what we will do is make sure that the services that the social media companies put in the checks that they need to," she told BBC News.

"That's our job, but the wider question about how everybody engages with this, it is for everybody, really.

"I actually think the real prize here is going to be for today's eight to 10-year-olds entering secondary school without it being the norm to go on Snap in your class group chat, without it being the norm to have all your sports fixtures organised on Instagram."

Ofcom's age verification report will now be considered by the government, with a decision due by the end of the year.

Child safety campaigners including the Molly Rose Foundation and NSPCC welcomed Ofcom's guidance.

But both said there were lessons to be learned from how Australia's social media ban had been implemented, after it was found many under-16s could still access social platforms.

"That's why, as we prepare to embark on our own social media ban in the UK, we need to make sure we accurately know the age of child users," said Rani Govender, head of child safety online at the NSPCC.

She said the government and Ofcom must ensure tech firms are held accountable for meeting age check standards "to help keep children safe online and ensure the ban delivers change in practice".

But Andy Burrows, the Molly Rose Foundation's chief executive, said Ofcom had shown a "dire track record" of enforcing the Online Safety Act - raising questions over how effectively it would help deliver a social media ban.

"Andy Burnham must deliver a ban that learns the lessons from Australia and that incentivises safety-by-design as the price of admission to the UK market, with a ban as the starting point in a proper plan to give children a safe and happy online life," he said.

Jonny Blunt, corporate affairs director of BT's consumer division, said families should "prepare children for life online after the ban and highlight the risks of trying to dodge the restrictions".

"Having those conversations now and giving young people time to prepare for the changes in March will be crucial in helping them adapt to a significant change for a whole generation," he said.

"The restrictions have the potential to change the way young people interact with the digital world for the better, but only if regulators, tech companies, families, and educators come together to make it a success."

Additional reporting by Liv McMahon and Chris Vallance

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself 'leader of Brazil' after election loss
articles.text:
The defeated candidate in Brazil's presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro, has referred to himself as "leader of Brazil" in a letter he published on social media after leaving the country for the United States.

Bolsonaro lost to his left-wing rival, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in the run-off on Sunday by a difference of 4.4 million votes, but has not conceded defeat.

In the letter, Bolsonaro alleges, without offering evidence, that he was the victim of "electoral fraud" and says that he will lead the opposition from the US.

He left Brazil on Tuesday after failing to comply with an order to surrender his passports, a decision which Lula described as "a shameful act".

Bolsonaro starts his letter, which he posted on his X account, saying "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the leader of Brazil".

However, he had posted a previous version, that was later deleted, in which he wrote: "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the rightful president of Brazil."

Both versions repeat the allegation that Bolsonaro first made on election night, that an extension of polling hours on Sunday had benefited his rival.

In the letter, he says it was "an electoral fraud unfolding before my eyes".

The extension was requested by both Lula's and Bolsonaro's campaign teams, and the head of Brazil's electoral authority has said that the vote proceeded normally and in full accordance with the country's laws and constitution.

An analysis of election data conducted by BBC Brazil and BBC Verify has also found that only around 34,000 people voted during the extended hours - far lower than the 4.4 million votes that separated Lula from Bolsonaro.

In his letter, Bolsonaro also addresses his departure from Brazil - which caused confusion after he disappeared for more than 24 hours.

It later emerged that he had gone across the land border to Argentina, and from there flew on to Florida, following a brief refuelling stop in Ecuador.

Bolsonaro left after failing to hand in his passports to police - in defiance of a Supreme Court order, which had been issued as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering.

He has not been charged as part of the money laundering probe and denies any wrongdoing, calling the investigation a "politically-motivated witch hunt".

Bolsonaro added that he had never intended to leave Brazil, but argued that he was the victim of "political persecution".

He ended the letter by saying: "I left Brazil but I haven't abandoned Brazilians".

The Trump administration has provided visas for Flávio Bolsonaro and his family but did not say what kind of visas they were.

The US president did not explicitly endorse Bolsonaro in the run-up to the election and told reporters he "won't get involved" when asked about Bolsonaro's allegations of election fraud.

Earlier in the week, he had said that "it looked like another rigged election," without providing any evidence.

And on Thursday, Trump told reporters that "the election was a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil".

articles.title: Ben Duckett and Liam Dawson impress as England beat Sri Lanka to end tri-series
articles.text:
One-day international tri-series, Lahore

England 386-5 (50 overs): Duckett 167 (132); Asitha 2-63

Sri Lanka 331 (45.1 overs): Rathnayake 118 (77); Dawson 4-49

England won by 55 runs

Ben Duckett's sublime century and four wickets for Liam Dawson earned England a consolation win over Sri Lanka in their final match of the tri-series.

Duckett struck a majestic 167 from 132 balls as England racked up 386-5 in Lahore, which set up a tantalising chase after Sri Lanka's astonishing pursuit of 430 in their previous encounter a week ago.

In another high-scoring match with very little contest between bat and ball, the chase followed a similar trajectory, as Sri Lanka kept themselves within touching distance of the run-rate throughout and needed 87 off the final 10 overs.

But England's bowlers held their nerve on this occasion, closing out a 55-run win as the brilliant Pavan Rathnayake's 118 off just 77 balls was in vain for Sri Lanka.

Rathnayake, who made 130 in last week's carnage, set the platform alongside Kusal Mendis' 89 but Sri Lanka lost their last five wickets for just 16 runs, with Dawson claiming the key scalp of Rathnayake in the 45th over as they were all out for 331.

It meant Duckett's second consecutive century eclipsed Rathnayake's effort, as England's opener capitalised on a batting-friendly surface and a tiring Sri Lanka attack.

The opening partnership between Duckett and Tom Banton impressed again as the pair added 163 together before the latter frustratingly dragged on to his stumps for a fine 74.

Duckett kicked on to his highest ODI score and though England fell short of the 400 mark, contributions of 44 from Harry Brook, 30 from Will Jacks and a quickfire 43 off 27 from Jordan Cox ensured they still posted a commanding total.

Such is the power of England's middle order that Root was not required to bat.

It was far from ideal for Sri Lanka's bowlers to toil in the heat as they face Pakistan in the tri-series final on Sunday, while England travel to Australia for three ODIs and five T20s in November.

While Duckett's 105 against Pakistan held a poor England innings together, here he was ruthless.

With very little swing or seam movement on offer, Duckett was able to back himself to flay anything wide of the off stump and timed the ball exquisitely off his pads when Sri Lanka were forced to bowl straighter.

They attempted to test with the short ball, too, but he was particularly prolific against it as the seamers lacked the pace to really trouble him.

It was also an impressive display of fitness from a player who has spoken about how hard he has worked at that part of his game, eventually falling in the 42nd over from a miscued ramp as the fatigue appeared to take its toll.

Duckett seems to relish opening with Banton: the pair have stands of 143, 6, 91, 74, 4 and 163 in their past six outings together. That, and Banton's form, has given England's selectors an intriguing conundrum for when Jacob Bethell returns from injury in Australia.

Bethell previously occupied the opening slot alongside Duckett but Banton, with five scores of fifty plus in his past six knocks, looks likely to have nailed down his place on this tour, despite some frustration that he could not kick on to three figures when conditions were so favourable.

"You want options, and guys to push their case when they get their opportunities," England coach Brendon McCullum told Sky Sports after the game.

"They're good problems for us to have. We will learn more about that in Australia, but we will always do what's right for the team depending on conditions and the opposition."

Bethell's versatility could potentially see him find a place in the middle order, but it is a promising indication of England's impressive white-ball depth that it is unclear who he could replace from Root, Brook and Jacks, with Jordan Cox needed as keeper in Jos Buttler's injury absence.

articles.title: Arsenal's Max Dowman to miss three matches after red card appeal rejected
articles.text:
Arsenal's Max Dowman will miss three matches after an appeal against his sending-off during Tuesday's Carabao Cup loss at Fleetwood was rejected.

The 16-year-old midfielder was shown a straight red card in the 85th minute after reacting to a heavy challenge by Fleetwood's Harrison Neal.

Although Dowman did not fully kick out, his foot did make contact with Neal.

The game finished 1-1 before League Two Fleetwood beat the Premier League champions 5-3 on penalties.

Arsenal appealed Dowman's sending-off on Wednesday.

It was Dowman's second red card this month having also been sent off while representing England's Under-19s.

As Dowman left the field, Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta gave him a scathing look and made what appeared to be an angry comment to the young winger.

Arteta said after the game: "When we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to respect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate. It was very clear."

Dowman was dismissed for violent conduct, which according to the laws of the game is when a player "uses or attempts to use excessive force or brutality against an opponent when not challenging for the ball... regardless of whether contact is made".

The Gunners were already light on options on the wing as Bukayo Saka, Christos Tzolis and Noni Madueke are currently out injured.

articles.title: Premier League to League One - is double drop becoming more common?
articles.text:
One day Leicester were playing Liverpool in the Premier League, then within 15 months it was Notts County, Burton Albion and MK Dons in League One.

It is a path of back-to-back relegations to the third tier of English football which was exceptionally rare. Now statistically it is becoming more common.

With Burnley marooned in the Championship relegation zone, they could be the third team in three years to suffer the double drop,

For the 1,450 Burnley supporters who made the trip to Lincoln City last weekend, the threat is all too real.

Head coach Nicky Hayen was never likely to survive a 4-1 defeat by a Lincoln team who were in non-league football 10 years ago.

With Diego Lopez appointed as Burnley's new chief football officer, and Fabio Celestini installed as their new boss, the Clarets must now hope for a change in fortunes.

Is the Championship becoming ever-more competitive as well-run clubs like Lincoln make an impact?

Or it simply a case of clubs from the Premier League imploding after relegation?

Fifteen years ago, the suggestion a top-flight club could be relegated in successive seasons was unthinkable.

After all, in the first 20 seasons of the Premier League it happened just the once.

That was to Swindon Town, and even then there were special circumstances.

The Robins finished fourth bottom of the second tier in 1994-95 but were relegated because of the rebalancing of the divisions to reduce the Premier League to 20 teams.

In any other season they would not have suffered the double drop.

As such, it could be argued that Wolves were the first team to suffer a double drop from the Premier League after being relegated in 2011-12.

Since then it has happened four times in 14 seasons.

Or, after Sunderland went down in 2016-18, three times in nine seasons.

And then back-to-back seasons with Luton and Leicester.

Meanwhile, Wigan and Portsmouth were relegated to League One after a second season in the Championship, Leeds and Sheffield Wednesday after a third.

For Wolves, Sunderland and Leicester there was considerable turmoil on and off the pitch which contributed to their demise.

Burney fans may fear there are similarities at Turf Moor.

During their double drop descent, Wolves - who remarkably suffered a treble drop to the bottom tier in the 1980s - burned through four managers and made a series of poor transfers.

Sunderland did so with the ignominy of being the only club to finish bottom of both divisions, winning just 13 of 84 league matches.

The Black Cats had been in the top flight for 10 seasons - though they had only reached the 40-point barrier, usually the target to remain in the division, three times.

Leicester's relegation to League One was a direct result of poor boardroom decisions, with a six-point deduction for breaching profit and sustainability regulations ultimately sealing their fate. The Foxes finished 23rd in the Championship, five points from safety.

It took Sunderland four years to return to the Championship, and such is the turmoil at Leicester an immediate promotion looks unlikely. Russell Martin's Leicester side sit 11th in League One, with the club up for sale.

"Despite the fact we've seen Luton and Leicester suffer back-to-back relegations in recent years, I don't see it as a trend that will continue," former Watford and Reading midfielder Jobi McAnuff, now an EFL pundit, told BBC Sport.

"For both of those clubs, in my opinion, it was a case of mismanagement of the playing squad.

"From Luton's perspective, there were a few players there who maybe felt an entitlement to stay in the Premier League. They didn't readjust to being back at the Championship, where most of their players had actually been previously.

"And for Leicester City, they kept hold of too many that didn't really want to be there and then obviously weren't equipped to deal with a relegation battle."

While Luton may have got their recruitment wrong, they were much more responsibly run compared to the other double drop clubs.

The Hatters' progress off the pitch remains progressive rather than regressive, with work advancing on a new 25,000-capacity stadium at Power Court which is due to be completed for the start of 2028-29.

The fine line for success is shown by Luton's relegation from the Championship in 2024-25. They went down because of their inferior goal difference compared to Hull City, with the Tigers then promoted to the Premier League the following season.

Burnley had earned a reputation as the archetypal yo-yo club - relegated from or promoted to the top division in each of the past five seasons.

But after a leveraged buyout by Alan Pace's ALK Capital in 2020, the Clarets were carrying £142m in loans in the 2024-25 accounts - the year they went up - which was the highest debt level in the Championship.

This week Burnley set a new English league record for the longest run without a home win. When they host Portsmouth on Saturday, it will be 378 days since their last home victory.

Being humbled by a well-run, up-and-coming club like Lincoln, with far fewer resources but savvy ownership, will not be lost on Burnley supporters.

And the financial gap is huge.

Burnley's total revenue for 2024-25 was £71.7m, which dwarfed Lincoln's £7.81m.

The Clarets then received £48m in parachute payments. Lincoln can expect about £5.5m in solidarity funding.

Off the pitch there should be no contest, but football is not played purely on balance sheets.

In its State of the Game report, published earlier this month, the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) said a new financial deal between the Premier League and the EFL must "reduce the distortive impact that parachute payments have on financial incentives within the Championship".

The solution is merit payments, which would mirror the Premier League's model of prize money by final league position.

At present, every club in the Championship receives the same payment, regardless of where they finish.

"The amount of money paid in parachute payments will reduce and the amount of money going into the Championship will vastly increase," IFR chair David Kogan said.

"The delta between parachute payment clubs and non-parachute payment clubs is going to significantly reduce, which makes the Championship a much more competitive league."

Parachute payments are paid to clubs relegated from the Premier League to help them adjust to the financial realities of the second tier - £48m in year one, then £39m in year two,

Could this make the double drop more common as the revenue gap closes? Much will depend upon just how "significantly" the gap is closed.

The IFR report found that parachute payment clubs were more than four times more likely to be promoted. In 2024-25, four clubs were in receipt and they were almost 27 points better off, and filled the top three places (with Luton relegated).

"If you look at the numbers of teams that go back up or finish in the top places, there's a huge correlation between those clubs and the ones that are parachute payment clubs," McAnuff said.

"Even with a reduction in parachute payments, I still feel that advantage will prove to be massively significant for those teams.⁠​⁠‍⁠"

It may yet be that Burnley escape the double drop, that the financial advantage of parachute payments outweighs poor decision-making.

But the double drop has generally become far more common. And that should concern any club that gets relegated and is not prepared for life in the Championship.

articles.title: South Africa vs Australia: Careless dismissals give tourists route to series win
articles.text:
Third Test, Cape Town (day three of five)

South Africa 329 & 140-4: Ackerman 62; Starc 2-29

Australia 429: Inglis 102; Harmer 4-104

South Africa lead by 40 runs

Batters carelessly gifting wickets to Australia... we have been here before.

This time it was not England helping their opponents, although they will have taken note with a tour of South Africa to come this winter.

South Africa's attempt to fight back in the decisive third Test against Australia was hurt by two poor strokes on day three.

Having taken the last six Australian wickets for 99 runs in the morning despite Josh Inglis' second Test century, the Proteas began their second innings facing a deficit of exactly 100.

They needed runs from their experienced opener and number three. Neither Aiden Markram nor David Bedingham could deliver.

By the end, even captain Temba Bavuma had been tempted into a wild swipe to fall for 35. South Africa were 140-4, just 40 runs ahead, at the close.

Australia are closing in.

In isolation, Markram's drive off Mitchell Starc straight into the hands of mid-off for one appeared the most egregious.

The ball was the fullest of the six balls Markram faced but not there for him to play his trademark shot. Fielder Travis Head did not have to move.

Worse, though, was the dismissal of Bedingham, who showed he had not learned from the first innings.

Then, the right-hander top-edged a pull to Josh Hazlewood off the bowling of Starc. This time he repeated the shot, with Hazlewood the wicket-taking bowler.

"That is just absolutely soft from David Bedingham," said former South Africa bowler Vernon Philander.

"He knew they were going to target him in that zone. For the second time in the Test, he has fallen to the same ploy."

Given the prized position in South Africa's batting order on the back of strong domestic form for Durham in the County Championship and twin hundreds for Western Province in September, this score of 11 followed contributions of 49, 46 and 50 in his other four innings.

He has got in but has not made a match-winning contribution.

Batting in the key position of first drop, some would say that is more infuriating than not getting in at all.

His dismissal, again like in the first innings, came shortly after being hit by a bouncer, with Starc clattering one into his chest on this occasion.

When, after starting with two balls on a good length, Hazlewood went short again, Bedingham's eyes lit up.

Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer and co should have been taking note. It was the fifth time he has been dismissed pulling in his 18 Tests.

On average he gets out playing that shot once every 13 deliveries.

"He never looks in the right position to play the pull or hook shot," former South Africa captain Graeme Smith said. "He is always off balance. He is never in a strong position.

"You think about best pullers in the game they have a strong base. He is pirouetting on one leg.

"[South Africa great] Hashim Amla just put the pull shot away for a phase.

"That is what a player like Bedingham needs to think about."

Bavuma, in contrast, dug in for 115 balls in which he hit only one boundary.

As he had in his 179 in the second-Test win in Gqeberha which set up this grand Cape Town finale, he showed his side the way in a partnership lasting 17.3 overs with Matthew Breetzke after opener Marques Ackerman had briskly made 65 before being bounced out by Starc.

But with four minutes to go in the day, Australia captain Pat Cummins tweaked his field for spinner Nathan Lyon.

Bavuma had pushed and driven outside off stump to that point but, with a silly point now in place, he was dragged from his crease and tried to force through mid-wicket.

Australia's celebrations suggested they believe that was the crucial wicket.

The vicious turn Lyon found means any chase over 200 would not be straightforward for Australia. South Africa's spinner Simon Harmer dismissed Inglis and Alex Carey (80) earlier in the day on his way to figures of 4-104.

The Proteas have Breetzke and Ryan Rickelton at the crease - and Test triple-centurion Wiaan Mulder to come, before in-form all-rounder Marco Jansen and the tail.

This still appears a tall order, however.

As on day one and two, Australia have held firm and their opponents faltered. England know that feeling too.

articles.title: Mexico City Grand Prix: Kimi Antonelli to miss media day with illness
articles.text:
Kimi Antonelli is to miss Thursday's Mexico City Grand Prix media day with an illness as he stands on the brink of clinching his first world title.

The Italian's Mercedes team said that Antonelli had a "viral illness" and had been excused his duties on Thursday by governing body the FIA "as a precaution to give him the chance to rest ahead of the weekend".

A Mercedes spokesperson said: "We expect him to be back tomorrow."

Practice for the race starts on Friday at 18:30 GMT.

Antonelli will seal the championship, and become the youngest winner in Formula 1 history, as long as he does not lose more than two points to team-mate George Russell and one point to Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton in the grand prix on Sunday.

The only way he could be stopped from tying up the title is if one of Russell and Hamilton wins. Ninth would be enough for Antonelli to become champion if it is Russell, and 10th if it is Hamilton.

Antonelli is one of two drivers to miss media day with an illness.

The other is Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas, who his team said was "unwell".

A Cadillac spokesperson said: "The team has taken the decision to allow him a day of rest, to support his recovery.

"This is a precautionary measure and does not currently affect his participation in the remainder of the race weekend. We will continue to monitor the situation and provide updates if necessary."

On Wednesday, Cadillac announced a new contract for the Finn's team-mate Sergio Perez, who will stay with the team until at least 2029.

They made no mention of Bottas' future in the announcement, and are said by insiders to be considering whether to promote their American reserve driver Colton Herta into F1.

Herta is having his fifth outing of the year in practice on Friday at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, as the team seek to earn him enough mileage to secure the so-called super licence that is required to race in F1.

Herta, previously a front-runner in the US-based Indycar championship, moved to Formula 2 this year with the intention of preparing himself for F1.

His season has not gone well and he is currently 19th in the standings with a best result of fifth place.

However, Cadillac feel he has shown more potential in his F1 outings, which also include a number of runs in cars from previous years.

No decision has been made on whether Bottas or Herta will partner Perez in 2027.

articles.title: Bruno Fernandes to remain Man Utd captain, says Michael Carrick
articles.text:
Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says Bruno Fernandes is "fully committed" to the club and will continue as captain.

Carrick dropped Fernandes to the bench for Sunday's 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after the Portuguese questioned the tactics used in a 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como.

The defeat by Bournemouth left Carrick's future hanging by a thread, but the 45-year-old will be in charge for Saturday's trip to Chelsea.

It remains to be seen whether Fernandes will return to the starting line-up, but the pair held clear-the-air talks at United's Carrington training ground on Tuesday in a bid to move forward.

Carrick says there is "no decision to be made" over whether Fernandes remains captain.

"We are clear with the situation of the team, and as a football club," said Carrick.

"He [Fernandes] is an important player for this group. He has been and he will be.

"We've got to make a difference and we've got to push things in a good direction.

"He's fully committed to this football club; he's fully committed to making things better. There are absolutely no issues with that.

"It doesn't change for me. It was a decision for what we felt for the [Bournemouth] game. That's it.

"He's the one that's led the team so well for many a game and many a year, and he'll continue to do that. There are absolutely no issues with that."

articles.title: Sergio Garcia targets Ryder Cup return as he confirms LIV exit to rejoin DP World Tour
articles.text:
Sergio Garcia has become the latest big name to quit LIV Golf while targeting a return to Europe's Ryder Cup team.

The one-time major champion said he will play on the Europe-based DP World Tour in 2027.

"This tour has been a huge part of my career from the beginning and I'm proud to call it home again," he said in a statement on social media., external

The 46-year-old Spaniard added: "I'm also keeping my options open for a return to the PGA Tour."

Garcia won a combined 27 titles on the American and European circuits between 1999 and 2020, including the 2017 Masters.

He joined LIV in June 2022 after it launched as a Saudi Arabia-backed project but the former world number two will not be part of the second phase of the breakaway circuit.

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing in April - having invested more than $5bn (£3.8bn) - leading to LIV filing for bankruptcy protection in the United States last month.

The league has secured a possible $300m (£224m) in financing to try to move forward with 'LIV 2.0' but only a handful of players have so far committed to the proposed competition in 2027.

Garcia follows top players Jon Rahm, Ian Poulter, Tyrrell Hatton and Graeme McDowell in announcing his departure.

In his statement, Garcia added that "the most exciting part for me is strengthening personal relationships, both new and old".

Garcia was sanctioned by the DP World Tour for breaking its rules when he defected to LIV, making him ineligible for the 2023 Ryder Cup.

The event's record points scorer had to settle outstanding fines - reported to be more than £1m - in order to be eligible for the 2025 edition, although ultimately he was not selected.

After helping Europe to six wins from 10 Ryder Cup appearances, he now hopes to return to their camp at Ireland's Adare Manor next year as a player or vice-captain.

"Another goal is to make that Ryder Cup team, and to be an asset to the guys in whatever capacity that may be," he said.

However, according to the current tour rules, while Garcia is eligible to play again, he cannot serve as a future captain or vice-captain.

Garcia may also face an awkward reunion with the PGA Tour.

Just before leaving for LIV in 2022, he told a rules official at the Wells Fargo Championship: "I can't wait to leave this tour. A couple more weeks and I won't have to deal with you any more."

He has remained eligible to play in majors and after hitting a poor shot at this year's Masters, Garcia ⁠slammed his driver into the Augusta turf and hit a nearby cooler, snapping the ​head ⁠off his club.

He apologised at the time and has now added: "There are some great tournaments around the world to play before Augusta next April, and I can't wait to get back to the Masters.

"I left Augusta last year disappointed with myself and my actions, and I'm ready to show what I've learned and where I am mentally.

"Augusta has given me some of the greatest moments of my life, and I'd love nothing more than to chase another green jacket at such a special place."

articles.title: Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end
articles.text:
The first tentative steps to end the 3pm television blackout in the UK have been taken by Scottish football as it seeks offers for the next broadcast cycle.

The SPFL has said that it is "flexible about the number of games" that will form part of the new deal, which will kick in from the 2029-30 season.

BBC Sport understands this includes the possibility that broadcasters could bid to show all matches live - including those shown on a Saturday afternoon.

The SPFL has created a tender with the greatest flexibility on the basis that the broadcaster does not seek to impose Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes.

Article 48 allows leagues to set specific times when matches are banned from being shown live on television. It can only be enforced when 50% of matches in a country's top two divisions are played at the same time.

While other parts of Europe have experimented with a blackout, it is now only present in the UK between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday.

Other leagues now tend to stagger kick-off times so the top divisions do not all play at the same time, meaning the blackout could not be applied.

In the UK, 3pm remains the traditional, default kick-off time for all leagues from the very top down through non-league.

It was introduced due to fears that televised games at 3pm could affect attendances, not just at the clubs involved but at those down the divisions too.

But as streaming has grown in popularity, critics have argued that it hinders the ability of clubs to exploit this revenue stream.

This is especially the case in the lower levels, which have had to adhere to the blackout and not show any of their games online.

In August, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters indicated the direction of travel was to end the blackout, but any decision would be 18 months away and taken in consultation with the EFL and the FA.

The upcoming broadcast cycle provides a unique opportunity for all leagues to come together and reach a consensus, as the rights deals for the Premier League, EFL and SPFL all end in 2028-29.

While the possibility to take all games is on the table in Scotland, it is by no means certain the option will be taken up.

Under the current terms, Sky Sports can show up to 60 Premiership matches a season, with Premier Sports showing up to 22.

In total, there are 228 games in the top flight, meaning only 36% of matches are shown live under the current broadcast deal.

The tender allows broadcasters to present any proposition for live coverage they see fit.

Any decision would then be up to the Premiership's 12 member clubs, with eight votes required to approve a deal.

Clubs could potentially opt to reject an offer which would include the Saturday 3pm games.

Scotland ending the 3pm blackout would not automatically mean English, Welsh and Northern Irish football follows suit.

articles.title: Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid: Are Mourinho's tactics misunderstood?
articles.text:
Barcelona fans have long teased Jose Mourinho, with their insult of choice being traductor - Spanish for translator.

It is their way of mocking the Real Madrid manager's humble beginnings.

Learning his future trade while serving as an interpreter for the legendary Sir Bobby Robson, Mourinho followed Robson from Sporting to Porto, before the pair reached Barcelona in 1996.

Four years later Mourinho was the manager of Benfica, the first steps in a coaching career that would lead him to Champions League glory, twice, and success in England, Italy and Spain.

So much more than merely a translator, even while at Barcelona, the Portuguese boss' wide and varied success best illustrates the true qualities that underpin him - diligent, determined, introspective, able to thrive in chaos, and tactically brilliant.

Last weekend, that eager tactical mind was in full force as Real Madrid beat Barcelona 2-1.

As the footballing world praised the tactics Mourinho used, it was an apt moment to reflect on his 26 years in management.

This Clasico featured Real Madrid playing in a 4-4-2 shape with winger Vinicius Jr suspended.

Federico Valverde played at right-back. Bernardo Silva came into the side partnering Aurelien Tchouameni in midfield. Arda Guler and Yan Diomande manned the flanks and Jude Bellingham played up top alongside Kylian Mbappe.

Like he has often done in big games, Mourinho asked one of his more industrious players, Silva on this occasion, to man-mark Barcelona's Pedri. Not an easy task, but it was one that minimised the Spaniard's influence.

Masterminding individual wins in big games tend to garner Mourinho warranted praise, but his wider approach does not always get the recognition it probably deserves.

In recent years, coaches with more clearly defined tactics, patterns of play, or fixed positional references have been lauded as the geniuses of the sport.

Mourinho hasn't taken this approach, opting for one that leans on the quality of his players and tactics that look different depending on the club he finds himself leading.

This less fixed style is more difficult to analyse from the outside looking in, which can result in misunderstanding his work entirely.

Mourinho is a follower of tactical periodisation, a way of football thinking pioneered by Vitor Frade.

While Mourinho was working alongside Robson at Porto in the mid-1990s, Frade was also part of the coaching staff.

Pulling on threads from psychology, sociology, neuroscience, and systems theory, Frade's thinking rejected the common belief that technical, tactical, physical and psychological parts of football should be treated as separate things.

Part of the thinking behind this was that these factors were not drawn on separately in a match but instead all at once.

When Mourinho took charge of Real for this season, the Athletic reported that training sessions had become shorter but more intense, always carrying a focus on the ball.

Even getting players match fit was a job done with the ball at their feet.

In recent seasons, there has been a rise in man-to-man pressing which has removed the ability for teams to find overloads. Pressing puts pressure on the attackers on the ball which hurries their decisions, too.

This has made games look more chaotic, which may be to Mourinho's benefit.

Students of Frade believe chaos is inseparable from the game. By training in a holistic manner, the hope is that players become better equipped to solve problems on the fly.

Perhaps this is why Mourinho's teams have typically thrived in difficult conditions, as underdogs, when the stakes have been high, or when games move away from pre-planned patterns.

Mourinho doesn't seek to control every decision his players make but instead looks to prepare them to find solutions for themselves; with better players, these solutions should, in theory, be better.

articles.title: Jake Paul: American to return to ring on 24 December in Dubai
articles.text:
Jake Paul will return to the ring for the first time since losing to Anthony Joshua against a yet to be confirmed opponent on 24 December.

American Paul had two titanium plates fitted and some teeth removed after Joshua broke his jaw during their heavyweight bout in December 2025.

The 29-year-old influencer said in May that his boxing career was "most definitely" in doubt.

Paul will headline a card in Dubai on Christmas Eve, with several names understood to be in contention to be his opponent.

"I've spent years proving people wrong, taking risks, and pushing myself against opponents nobody thought I'd face," Paul said.

"Nothing that's happened has changed my belief in myself or what I'm working toward. I'm hungrier than ever.

"We've got plenty of names on the list; let's see who signs the contract. Merry Christmas, Dubai. Santa Paul is coming to town, and somebody's getting knocked out."

Paul has won 12 of his 14 fights as a professional, with his two defeats coming against Tommy Fury and Joshua.

articles.title: Man Utd crisis: Sometimes a manager needs sacking for their own good - Gary Neville
articles.text:
Gary Neville says managers sometimes need to be sacked "for their own good" as he reflected on Manchester United's decision to persist with under-pressure Michael Carrick.

United are 16th in the Premier League, just one point above the relegation zone, following a dismal 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on Sunday.

Carrick was widely expected to be sacked after that loss, but the club have opted to give the 45-year-old head coach the opportunity to turn things around, and he will remain in charge for United's trip to Chelsea on Saturday lunchtime.

"I reckon what's happened in the 24 hours after Bournemouth is that they've literally debated it back and forth," former Manchester United captain Neville said on the Stick to Football podcast.

"I don't know this, but they've debated it to the point where they've got themselves into a muddle, and thought, 'we'll just stay with him'.

"I think staying with him is a result of the lack of planning, the lack of probably available options, the lack of decision-making around the two people that probably are available. That's when you're really struggling."

Neville added: "Sometimes a manager needs sacking for their own good. I needed sacking at Valencia. I was happy that they put me out of my misery."

Carrick's position was precarious even before the Bournemouth game after captain Bruno Fernandes criticised the tactics deployed in the 4-1 Champions League loss at Como last week.

Fernandes was dropped for the Bournemouth match, but he and Carrick have since held talks to clear the air.

"We've all been in football dressing rooms, and they're quite brutal places," Neville said.

"If Bruno Fernandes, the captain of the club... if he comes out and questions the manager's tactics after a 4-1 defeat in Como, where he's played like a drain, and he's been playing like a drain for three months, and the rest of them have as well, that is only 1 or 2% of what they're actually saying internally."

United fans sang Carrick's name as he applauded the crowd after the Bournemouth defeat during what Neville called "effectively a farewell lap".

Those fans then booed the players as soon as Carrick went down the tunnel.

articles.title: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
articles.text:
Andy Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill "as soon as we possibly can", but was unable to guarantee this would happen before the next general election.

Opponents raised concerns over the lack of details on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, after welfare spending was forecast to increase from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2031/32.

Asked whether he would seek to reduce the bill before the next election, Burnham told reporters: "We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we're working flat out to that end."

He warned against "crude cuts" and said he wants to get people into "sustainable employment". The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare".

The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".

The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.

Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.

These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.

The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.

Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.

He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."

Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.

"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."

articles.title: What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?
articles.text:
Chancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have both spoken of their desire for the benefits bill to come down, but the government has not yet laid out a timetable for any reductions.

Their political opponents have criticised them for a lack of detail on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, accusing the government of delaying difficult decisions over cuts.

Official forecasts released alongside the Budget indicate welfare spending is going to increase by £79bn in cash terms over the next few years.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the numbers behind this thorny political issue and some of the difficult options the government have to bring down welfare costs.

The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), estimates in its latest forecasts that the cost of the welfare system will rise, external from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032.

The OBR's figures include spending on pensioners, which accounts for just under half of the total. The majority of this cost is on the state pension.

However, if we look at the size of welfare spending relative to the size of the overall economy the OBR's projections are less dramatic, increasing from 11.1% today to 11.3% of GDP in 2032.

Total welfare spending would also remain below the peak of around 12% of GDP in 2013 following the global financial crisis, leading some economists and researchers to question the idea that welfare spending is out of control., external

But there are some welfare costs that are rising rapidly.

Spending on health and disability related benefits, in particular Personal Independence Payments (PIP), is up sharply since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Accounting for inflation, spending on working-age disability benefits increased from £14bn in 2020 to £25bn in 2026, external.

Inflation-adjusted welfare spending remains lower than 2013 because several other working-age benefits, such as Universal Credit and housing benefit, were cut by Conservative-led governments as part of their austerity programme from 2010 onwards, external.

So spending in some parts of the system has come down while it has risen in others - and there could be a connection.

Some researchers think the post-2010 welfare cuts to benefits might have created an incentive for people to claim sickness and disability benefits instead to protect their living standards, external, therefore shifting costs around the system rather than generating lasting savings.

Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is leading an official review into Neets and is expected to recommend major reforms designed to get many off benefits and into work.

His interim report in May estimated that annual PIP expenditure on 16 to 24-year-olds rose from £1.3bn in 2020 to around £3.2bn in 2025, external. It also projected this cost would reach £6.5bn and cover 700,000 young people in five years' time.

PIP claimants can be in work, but official statistics show that only around one in five are, external.

Politicians are often unclear about what they mean by reducing spending on welfare.

In March 2025, former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer's government presented a plan which it said would save £5bn a year from health-related welfare spending by 2030 by tightening PIP access and reducing the value of health-related Universal Credit payments.

But official forecasts made it clear that annual spending on health-related welfare in cash terms was still set to rise after the reform, external, just not as rapidly as the path it had previously been on.

However, at the time the OBR did forecast the plans would help put overall UK welfare spending on a "slightly downward trajectory" as a share of the economy, external over the medium term, rather than remaining flat as had been previously projected.

So this type of relative reduction in anticipated welfare spending, rather than a cut in absolute cash terms, could be what the government seeks to deliver.

The final Milburn report is expected in the coming weeks, as well as a separate final report from disability minister Stephen Timms into the options for PIP reform.

There has been speculation that these could recommend creating a new welfare system for people under the age of 25, external, so they are not eligible for PIP and receive lower payments than older people.

There are also suggestions Timms could propose a new PIP eligibility test to reduce access, external, although he was not specifically instructed to find savings.

Reforms along these lines could potentially make some savings to the welfare bill relative to the existing trajectory of rising spending, as well as reducing forecast welfare spending as share of GDP.

But some analysts argue that to be effective in delivering sustainable savings, such reforms are likely also to require the government to spend a lot more, external to enable young people in particular to get into and remain in work.

This was signalled by the interim Milburn report which noted that for every £1 the government spends on employment support for young people around £25 is spent on benefits, suggesting he could propose a significant increase in government spending on welfare-to-work schemes.

This means that any welfare savings could, in the near term at least, be offset by additional spending in other departments.

However, in the long term this approach could still deliver welfare savings if the employment support was effective.

articles.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand options for customers
articles.text:
DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.

DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.

Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said.

"Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.

"Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.

For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said.

"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.

He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".

The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.

Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting.

"Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.

In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.

DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.

The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.

New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating."

"Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.

articles.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
articles.text:
Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.

Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."

"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added.

"We will update the public when more information is available."

The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.

The information was put in a database named Icepick.

Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE.

Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.

BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.

A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the group's work to hack DHS records.

"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.

Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security.

The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.

Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.

A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."

Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents.

In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.

Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.

Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, external, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people.

Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.

Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded, external DHS enforces the requirement.

articles.title: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs
articles.text:
Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.

On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).

Like many other major tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.

Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.

The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.

Big tech companies like Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure like data centres.

Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - up 19% from a year earlier - driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.

Its earnings were lifted by a 30% increase in revenue for Microsoft Cloud - its range of enterprise technology services.

The firm also flagged risks, including "substantial investments" in AI, among other uncertainties that could impact its finances.

The firm's chief executive Satya Nadella said AI development has helped grow the adoption of the technology and has delivered "real-world impact across every industry."

articles.title: Elon Musk a 'real genius', Putin says after talks with SpaceX boss
articles.text:
Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.

The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites.

"He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."

Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.

Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".

"We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.

Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.

The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field".

"Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.

Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Ukraine relied on Starlink internet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, something Musk has admitted SpaceX did intentionally.

US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia to import diesel in an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.

Then Trump waived certain sanctions against Russia that were set to take effect.

Not long after, a US citizen was released from Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".

Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.

articles.title: Drone technology: Start-ups look for ways to make quieter drones
articles.text:
Nature lover Ashley Schmidt no longer spends much time in her garden, in the Dallas suburb of North Garland.

She's also given up on cycling to the local parks where she previously enjoyed taking close-up photos of the bugs, lizards and toads.

It's all because she can't stand the sound of the delivery drones that fly overhead, depositing her neighbours' online orders.

"They emit this very annoying buzz. It triggers my fight or flight response," says the 44-year-old administrative assistant.

"You can hear the drones on approach and you can hear them inside your home when they pass directly overhead and then you hear them as they leave," she says.

Schmidt is one of a growing number of people living with the noise of drones dispatched by companies including Amazon and Walmart as they seek to speed up home deliveries.

Delivery drone services, not long ago a novelty, are becoming part of everyday life for many people in the US.

Among them, Amazon Prime Air is in the process of expanding deliveries to nearly 500 cities and towns, delivering items that fit into a space the size of a shoe box. It has also launched to customers in and around Darlington in the north of England.

Smaller drone delivery services are popping up too: in some US cities, customers can order flying treats from their local pizza joint or ice cream parlour.

Even in cities where noise is already a steady part of life, the sound of drones seems to irk in a particular way.

While the steady passing of traffic might blend into the background, the sudden whine of a drone's rotors can pierce the everyday hum.

The sound tends to be "particularly noticeable, even when overall sound levels are relatively low," says Antonio Torija Martinez, professor in acoustic engineering and psychoacoustics at the University of Salford.

Unlike planes, drones operate at low altitudes and may fly directly over residential areas.

"They can expose communities that have not previously experienced significant aircraft noise, and who may therefore be more sensitive to changes in their local soundscape," says Torija Martinez.

He points to research showing that people respond strongly to a noise when they consider the source to be "novel, intrusive or frequent". People who benefit from a drone delivery service, for example, may be less bothered by the noise.

However, complaints about the sound of drones are likely to grow, he warns: "At the moment we are seeing some of these problems localised in some areas, but… as the drone sector expands, more and more of these complaints will happen."

In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulates commercial drones, but it has come under fire for allowing noisy drone delivery operations. The FAA says operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for addressing any community concerns.

Might better technology muffle the irritating buzz?

One startup, Greenjets, set out to tackle both "noise level and the frequency of that noise," as Darren James, future technologies lead at the company, puts it.

The London-based business has designed a propulsion system it claims can reduce drone noise by at least two thirds.

While standard drones use spinning propellers that slice through open air, creating that high-pitched buzz, Greenjets encloses spinning blades inside a pod, to muffle the sound and direct the noise away from the ground.

Its system also quietens things down through slower rotor speed and by using materials that reduce vibration noise.

Making quieter drones isn't just about keeping the noise down for neighbours who are already sick of airborne deliveries.

Greenjets' low-noise tech has been used by police and harbour security teams in Germany. It has also helped conservationists in Africa, who are seeking to track poachers from above without being detected.

Battlefield drone operators also have good reason to keep the noise down, to avoid alerting the enemy of the approach of their unmanned vehicles.

"There are some efforts to reduce the sound of drones. The US Special Forces are interested, at an experimental stage," says Robert Tollast, a research fellow at Whitehall think tank The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

But he stresses that drone speed, rather than stealthiness, tends to come first for larger drones used in the war between Russia and Ukraine. "Make it faster, not less quiet, seems to be the approach," says Tollast.

For Detroit-based entrepreneur, Greg Sharrow, it was the challenge of broadcasting a classical music performance back in 2012 that set him on the path to quieter drone design.

He needed to film a violinist from a tricky angle and a drone seemed the only solution – except that it would be far too noisy.

As a starting point, "I knew that most of the noise from the drone was coming from the propeller, not the motor," he says. Specifically, it was the tips of the blades that he realised were creating the noise as they swiped through the air.

"I asked myself a very simple question, what would a tipless propeller look like and how would it function?"

The result was to create a propeller with twisted loop-shaped blades with no points.

It turned out it was easier to test his propeller in water than it was to repeatedly fly a drone, which led Sharrow to initially develop a less noisy boat propeller. Now, however, his company, Sharrow Engineering, is focusing on developing "ultra-quiet" drone rotors.

"We have validated that the technology works in drone applications and that it is dramatically quieter," says Sharrow.

Companies at the forefront of drone deliveries say they are also working to reduce the noise of their fleets. A spokesperson for Amazon says it has made "measurable sound improvements" to its drones and its latest designs use custom-designed propellers "that produce almost half the perceived sound of the prior generation, with a milder tone".

Drone maker Wing, which provides its vehicles for Walmart deliveries, says its propellers are designed to minimise noise. It also varies its flight paths to prevent repeated overflights over any single home or neighbourhood.

For Schmidt, fed up with the noise of drones, the only truly satisfactory solution would be to halt drone deliveries in her area. "I would like them to completely stop until they figure out how their services stop being a nuisance," she says.

articles.title: iPhone Duo: Apple to replace handsets affected by screen issues
articles.text:
Apple has acknowledged some of its iPhone Duo handsets have developed problems with their screens, just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale.

Photos posted on social media show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device, which has a starting price of £1,999 ($2,668) in the UK.

Apple said it was aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of the phones and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement.

The Duo's launch, which attracted crowds at Apple stores around the world last week, is an attempt to reinvigorate the brand's device range and challenge the foldable phones made by rivals.

Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.

An iPhone Duo user, Justin Lokos, posted an image of a device with lines across the right side of the display and later uploaded a picture of a new handset alongside the broken one, thanking an Apple store in New York for its help.

The extent of the issue remains unclear. Apple did not say how many devices were affected, while some images showing faulty devices may have been created using AI.

Francisco Jeronimo, technology analyst at market research firm IDC, said that meant some caution was needed before drawing conclusions about the whole production run.

But he added the early reports of issues also showed "that even a company with Apple's engineering resources and supply chain discipline faces a steep learning curve in foldables".
